evidence: Colonic diverticula are acquired herniations of mucosa and submucosa through weak points in the muscular wall. Diverticulitis requires inflammatory change involving a diverticulum and the surrounding fat.
Diverticula without surrounding inflammation, commonly an asymptomatic incidental finding.
An inflamed diverticulum with focal bowel wall thickening and pericolic inflammatory change.
Diagnosis rests on the combination of an inflamed diverticulum, segmental wall thickening and pericolic inflammation, not on diverticula alone.
Contrast-enhanced CT confirms the diagnosis, grades severity and identifies complications.
Usually sufficient to assess the bowel wall, surrounding fat, abscesses and free fluid.
Oral or rectal contrast is generally unnecessary for standard assessment.
Marked short-segment asymmetric wall thickening, lymphadenopathy or absent typical peridiverticular inflammation should raise concern for colorectal cancer.
Once diverticulitis is identified, review the entire examination for complications and their extent.
Fluid collection with rim enhancement and often gas. Report size and potential accessibility.
Pericolic gas suggests contained perforation; free intraperitoneal gas and fluid indicate free perforation.
A tract or inflammatory adherence to an adjacent organ. Bladder gas without instrumentation suggests a colovesical fistula.
Describe narrowing, upstream dilatation and segment length; exclude malignancy.
Do not stop after naming diverticulitis: abscess size, free gas, fistula, stenosis and distant complications alter management.
Inflamed diverticulum, maximum wall thickness and extent of fat stranding.
Abscess in three dimensions, extraluminal gas, free fluid, fistula or obstruction.
State uncomplicated or complicated and provide the CDD type when confident.
For atypical patterns discuss cancer, colitis or epiploic appendagitis.
Example: Acute sigmoid diverticulitis with marked pericolic inflammation, without abscess or free perforation, consistent with CDD type 1b.
The images demonstrate the key distinction: local inflammation without a drainable collection versus complicated disease with abscesses.
Segmental sigmoid wall thickening, diverticula and marked pericolic stranding without free perforation or a drainable collection.
Rim-enhancing pericolic collections containing gas at the rectosigmoid junction indicate complicated diverticulitis.
01 Recognise the triad Diverticula, segmental wall thickening and pericolic stranding form the typical CT pattern.
02 Complications matter Actively search for and precisely describe abscess, perforation, fistula and stenosis.
03 Use CDD purposefully Classification supports the report; the key distinction is uncomplicated versus complicated.
04 Do not miss cancer Atypical focal or asymmetric thickening and lymphadenopathy require an oncological differential.
